records.title: refactor(api): rewrite org tree traversals as depth-guarded recursive CTEs
records.body:
Part of #855 — Phase 0. **This is the highest-risk work in the Epic.**

## Why

Three functions walk the org tree using a fixed number of aliased self-joins, one per level. They are correct only because the tree is currently exactly five deep. When it becomes six, they do not crash and do not log — they return quietly incomplete results, because a `LEFT JOIN` that runs out of tree returns `NULL` and the callers filter nulls away. A truncated chain is indistinguishable from a legitimately short one.

### 1. `checkHasRoleOnOrg` — ancestors

[`packages/api/src/check-has-role-on-org.ts:54`](https://github.com/F3-Nation/f3-nation/blob/main/packages/api/src/check-has-role-on-org.ts#L54) declares five aliases and climbs AO → region → area → sector → nation. With territory the chain is six, so the walk stops at sector: **nation admins silently lose implicit admin rights over AOs.**

Note the alias comments are also wrong today — `level_3_org` is commented `// Sector` and `level_4_org` is commented `// Area`, but joining upward from a region gives area at level 3 and sector at level 4. The labels are swapped. Harmless at runtime, but it is a fair sign of how hard this code is to reason about, and the replacement should not carry the confusion forward.

### 2. `getEditableOrgIdsForUser` — descendants

[`packages/api/src/get-editable-org-ids.ts:65`](https://github.com/F3-Nation/f3-nation/blob/main/packages/api/src/get-editable-org-ids.ts#L65) declares three aliases and descends from the user's own org. A sector admin's descent now ends at area: **regions disappear from their editable set.**

### 3. `getDescendantOrgIds` — descendants *(not in the original #855 audit)*

[`packages/api/src/get-descendant-org-ids.ts`](https://github.com/F3-Nation/f3-nation/blob/main/packages/api/src/get-descendant-org-ids.ts) is a third ladder, and has the widest blast radius of the three. Its own docstring says it traverses *"up to 5 levels deep"* — five aliases, `level_0` through `level_4`. From a nation, today's chain is exactly five, so it fits with nothing to spare. Add territory and it needs six: **AOs drop out of every descendant set.**

It has 8 call sites across six routers — `location.ts`, `event.ts`, `position.ts` (×2), `user.ts`, `org.ts` (×2), and `map/event.ts` — so the failure surfaces as events, locations, and positions going missing from list endpoints, not just as a permissions problem.

## What to build

Replace all three with depth-guarded recursive CTEs.

**Implementation note:** drizzle-orm is pinned at **0.45.2**, which does **not** expose `withRecursive`. This was verified against the installed package, not the docs. These must be written as raw `sql` templates.

Ancestors, validated against a live local database — it returned the full `ao → region → area → sector → nation` chain:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE ancestors AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, org_type, 0 AS depth FROM orgs WHERE id = $1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT o.id, o.parent_id, o.org_type, a.depth + 1
  FROM orgs o JOIN ancestors a ON o.id = a.parent_id
  WHERE a.depth < 20
)
SELECT id, org_type FROM ancestors;
```

Descendants are the same shape with the join inverted (`o.parent_id = d.id`); that form was also validated and correctly returned both areas and both regions beneath a sector. The `depth < 20` guard bounds runaway recursion if the data ever contains a cycle — worth keeping even though `orgs.parent_id` should make cycles impossible.

**The pattern already exists in this repo.** [`org-chart/index.ts:160`](https://github.com/F3-Nation/f3-nation/blob/main/packages/api/src/router/org-chart/index.ts#L160) `buildParentChain` walks the parent chain in a loop with cycle detection, and [`map-request-notification.ts:85`](https://github.com/F3-Nation/f3-nation/blob/main/packages/api/src/services/map-request-notification.ts#L85) `findParentOrgByType` recurses upward until it finds a given type. Both are already depth-agnostic and need no changes. We are not inventing an approach — we are applying the one already proven here to the three places that skipped it.

## Ordering — why this lands before territory exists

This work must land **while the hierarchy is still five levels deep**, so it can be proven behavior-preserving against known-good output. Rewriting authorization logic and changing the hierarchy in the same PR would leave no way to tell a rewrite bug from a hierarchy bug — and since both failure modes are silent, there would be nothing to debug from.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three functions use recursive CTEs with a depth guard; no `aliasedTable` ladders remain
- [ ] Tests prove **identical** results to the current implementations on the present five-level hierarchy, for each function
- [ ] Tests additionally cover a synthetic **six-level** fixture, asserting the deepest level is reached — these fail against the old implementation, which is the point
- [ ] Cycle-guard behavior is covered
- [ ] The 8 `getDescendantOrgIds` call sites are spot-checked; the callers' contracts are unchanged

records.title: architecture audit: reduce orchestration hotspots without product rewrites
records.body:
## Goal

Track **remaining** architecture/code-quality work that materially improves correctness, maintainability and boundary clarity without rewriting working product code for aesthetic purity.

Parent reconstruction program: #634. Cleanup/deletion routing: #289.

## Principles

- file size is evidence of pressure, not a refactor requirement;
- extract only stable responsibilities that change/test independently;
- prefer deleting duplication and using existing framework/platform ownership over adding abstractions;
- preserve public product/API/persistence behavior unless the bounded issue explicitly changes it;
- use focused issues/PRs as the work queue rather than a second architecture inventory document.

## Completed slices — do not redo

### ✅ Saved-Work cold-open query fan-out — #430

Merged #430 introduced the authorization-rooted `WorkBundleRepository`, bounding the ordinary populated Work graph to six DB executions while preserving response shape, authorization, signing, ordering and pagination/chunk safety.

The remaining architectural note from that work is narrow: the specialized read model reuses a private Job row codec. If this causes repeated cross-repository coupling, make persistence codecs an explicit reusable contract in a bounded follow-up; do not reopen the N+1 work.

### ✅ Auth/provider failure semantics — #537

Merged #537 distinguishes invalid credentials from retryable/provider/transport/local failures instead of collapsing every `sb.auth.get_user(...)` exception into 401/anonymous behavior. Required and optional auth now preserve the intended failure taxonomy with regression tests.

### ✅ Shared API-process service-role Supabase client — #621

Merged #621 removed the duplicate auth-side service-role singleton/env/lock/client construction. `auth_utils.get_supabase_client()` delegates to the repository-owned shared client, with process-identity, concurrent-first-access and missing-config regressions.

Do not reopen #556 or recreate another API-process Supabase client factory. Worker process client/config ownership can evolve independently with #645/#651 where appropriate.

### ✅ Shared observability bootstrap — #420

API/worker Sentry bootstrap is centralized in `observability.py`; do not reintroduce framework-specific duplicate initialization.

## Remaining verified hotspots

### P0/P1 — frontend server-state/application coordination

`app/page.tsx` remains a large application coordinator, but the highest-leverage deletion path is now #650:

- generated OpenAPI operations own wire contracts;
- TanStack Query owns generic remote cache/dedupe/retry/polling/invalidation;
- product-specific Work/Version/selection/transport invariants remain explicit.

Use #650 to remove custom server-state machinery first. Only then extract any remaining Work hydration/job lifecycle coordination from `page.tsx` if it still has an independent responsibility boundary. Do not create a second frontend service framework.

### P1 — backend capability composition hotspot

`backend/domain/capabilities.py` still mixes:

- persistence/storage helpers;
- progress adaptation;
- DSP/OSS fallback extraction;
- composite `understand` orchestration;
- individual capability handlers;
- registration/composition.

Do not split by LOC. Preferred sequence:

1. identify helpers used across multiple handler families;
2. extract one coherent persistence/job-I/O seam with focused tests;
3. extract handler families only where they have distinct dependency/verification boundaries;
4. leave registry/composition thin;
5. keep evaluation code out of production modules.

This work should also make #287 API-vs-worker dependency ownership easier rather than introduce new cross-imports.

### P1 — public workflow intent vs worker execution registry

#632 owns the concrete boundary bug: `/workflows/create` can currently queue arbitrary registered worker capability names. Worker registration must not imply public API exposure.

Fix that fail-closed contract before treating registration as an architectural extension point.

### P1/P2 — Python package/import ownership

`backend/pyproject.toml` still needs both `.` and `..` on pytest `pythonpath` because flat and package-qualified import styles coexist.

Normalize one convention deliberately across API, worker, tests and evaluation entrypoints, then remove the dual-root workaround. Import Linter from #639 comes **after** this graph is truthful, not before it.

### P1/P2 — configuration ownership

#645 now owns migration from scattered runtime `os.environ` parsing toward one small typed backend settings boundary while deployment remains the authority for effective production values.

Do not create a manually synchronized environment manifest or expose server config to the browser.

### P2 — CSS cascade/version strata

#523 owns the versioned global CSS stack. Consolidate only after selector/property ownership and browser/visual regressions identify superseded layers. Do not combine CSS archaeology with product redesign.

### P2 — persistence codecs

Repository/read-model code should not need to call another repository class's private `_row_to_*` helper. If repeated current-main callsites remain, expose a small explicit row codec/mapper contract rather than duplicating serialization or constructing a generic repository framework.

### P2 — dependency/runtime ownership

#287 owns API/common vs worker/ML vs evaluation dependency grouping. Keep one `pyproject.toml` + one `uv.lock`; do not solve dependency footprint with service/repository splits.

### P2 — bespoke platform infrastructure

Architecture cleanup should consume, not duplicate, the explicit replacement programs:

- #648 — native GitHub merge queue + one PR Gate, then delete cross-workflow polling/serialized integration;
- #650 — OpenAPI/TanStack Query convergence;
- #651 — evaluate PGMQ/Supabase Queues before retaining custom lease/recovery transport indefinitely;
- #639 — maintained static analyzers only after the

records.title: feat: Priority-ordered Arazzo file parsing (P2-7)
records.body:
## Summary
Add dependency-aware file ordering for multi-file Arazzo workspaces: discover all `.arazzo.yaml` files in a directory, build a file-level dependency graph (schemas before workflows that reference them), parse in order, and produce a combined document collection.

## Context
- Arazzo specs can span multiple YAML files (schemas in shared files, workflows in separate files)
- Files reference each other across boundaries (sourceDescriptions pointing to other .arazzo files, schema definitions referenced from workflow steps)
- Currently: no multi-file support exists in the runner
- The `DependencyGraph` class already does step-level topological sort within a single workflow — same pattern extends to file-level

## Scope (Grilled — agreed with user)

### Q1: Full Workspace DTO + Loader
- Directory discovery of all `.arazzo.yaml` files
- Build file-level dependency graph
- Parse files in dependency order
- Produce combined document collection

### Q2: Both cross-file reference patterns
- Schema definitions referenced from workflow steps (schemas in shared files, workflows in separate files)
- sourceDescriptions pointing to other .arazzo files (workspace-level sourcing)

### Q3: File-path-based error shape
- Cycles detected across files throw with file paths (not step IDs)
- New error shape: `FileParseCycleException` with file path context

### Q4: Separate FileResolver class with public API
- `FileResolver::parseAll(array<RawDocument> $docs): array<ArazzoDocument>`
- Public standalone class, Parser can delegate to it
- Callers (CLI, Laravel provider) can use it directly

## Files to create/modify
- `packages/core/src/Loader/FileResolver.php` (NEW) — topological sort + multi-file parsing
- `packages/core/src/Loader/Exceptions/FileParseCycleException.php` (NEW)
- `packages/core/src/Spec/Workspace.php` (NEW) — DTO holding multiple ArazzoDocuments
- Tests

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] FileResolver correctly sorts files by cross-file references (schemas before workflows)
- [ ] Cycles detected with file-path error context
- [ ] Both schema defs and sourceDescriptions handled as cross-file refs
- [ ] Workspace DTO holds parsed document collection
- [ ] All existing tests pass
- [ ] PHPStan level max passes
- [ ] Pint style passes

## Dependencies
None — independent. Can start immediately.

records.title: tech-debt: process_collector! mutates collector.objects while iterating it
records.body:
## Summary

`process_collector!` iterates `collector.objects` while the body inserts into that same `Dict`:

```julia
function process_collector!(collector::DeletionCollector)
  for (model, keys) in collector.objects
    find_related_objects!(collector, model, keys)   # -> handle_on_delete! -> add_objects_to_collector!
  end
  ...
```

`add_objects_to_collector!` does `collector.objects[model] = []` for every cascade target it
discovers, so new keys land in the `Dict` mid-iteration. Julia does not defend against this — it
neither raises nor snapshots — so the number of models visited, and the number of times each is
visited, depends on rehash timing.

No live database needed (mock connections).

## Reproduction of the underlying hazard

Julia's behaviour, measured directly:

```julia
d = Dict(i => i for i in 1:4)
for (k, v) in d; d[k+100] = v; end
length(d)   # 15, not 8 — the loop iterated keys it had inserted
```

The deletion collector's own fixture set is in
`test/unit/test_delete_multipath_alignment.jl` (`Dmp_root` / `Dmp_a` / `Dmp_b` / `Dmp_c` / `Dmp_k`),
which is a ready five-model cascade to experiment on.

## What is NOT claimed

**On the current code this does not produce a wrong plan on any fixture I could build.** Measured
after #452 landed, every statement in that fixture's plan emits exactly one top-level `IN (…)`
fragment per genuine cascade path:

```
dmp_k    fragments=2   markers=2   params=2
dmp_c    fragments=2   markers=2   params=2
dmp_b    fragments=2   markers=2   params=2
dmp_a    fragments=1   markers=1   params=1
```

A review pass reported `dmp_c` emitting three fragments with a duplicate; that measurement was
against the **pre-#452** code, where the multi-path branch wrapped the arms in a nested `Qor` that
reads as an extra fragment. It does not reproduce post-fix. This issue is about the code relying on
undefined iteration behaviour, not about a symptom on today's model sets.

## Why it is still worth fixing

The two failure modes are asymmetric, and one is silent:

- **Visited twice** → a redundant duplicate entry for a model, i.e. a redundant OR arm. Wasteful,
  not wrong: the arms are ORed, so the row set is unchanged.
- **Skipped** → a cascade target never collected, so its rows are never deleted. On PostgreSQL and
  SQLite the FK is `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` / deferred by pragma, so this surfaces as a
  constraint violation at COMMIT — loud, but only where a constraint exists. A model declaring
  `on_delete = CASCADE` against a table with no FK constraint would orphan rows silently.

Rehash thresholds mean the risk grows with the number of models in one cascade, which is exactly the
case least likely to be covered by a fixture.

## Suggested fix

Collect the work list before iterating, e.g. walk `collect(collector.objects)` (or a queue seeded
from it and drained as `find_related_objects!` appends), so insertion during traversal is explicit
rather than incidental. A `visited::Set{PormGModel}` guard would also close the double-visit half —
`find_related_objects!` currently has three recursion sites and no visited set.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `process_collector!` no longer mutates the collection it is iterating
- [ ] A cascade over enough models to force a `Dict` rehash mid-traversal collects every target
- [ ] Unit coverage on a model set large enough to exercise that path

## Related

- #452 — found while reviewing that fix; pre-existing and deliberately out of its scope.

records.title: [build-timings] Build Performance Report — 2026-08-26
records.body:
## Build Summary

- **Total build time**: 3m 30s (210.4s wall clock, `cargo build --workspace --timings`)
- **Compilation units**: 372 (including build scripts)
- **Direct dependencies**: 40 (`cargo tree --depth 1`)
- **Total dependency graph size**: ~820 lines (`cargo tree`)
- **Compiler**: rustc 1.98.0 (88d9e12ae 2026-08-18), cargo 1.98.0
- **clippy**: `cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings` — clean, zero warnings

## Top 5 Slowest Compilation Units

| Crate | Version | Duration | Start (s) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| aws-lc-sys | 0.40.0 | 93.86s | 16.06 | C build (BoringSSL/AWS-LC), pulled in transitively via jsonschema's default TLS backend |
| libgit2-sys | 0.17.0+1.8.1 | 71.69s | 120.00 | C build for git2; already scoped to default-features = false, features = ["https"] |
| syn | 2.0.117 | 27.02s | 4.27 | Proc-macro backbone; unblocks 15 downstream units — biggest critical-path blocker |
| ring | 0.17.14 | 23.28s | 85.93 | Crypto backend, duplicate TLS stack alongside aws-lc-rs |
| rustls | 0.23.37 | 22.00s | 171.09 | TLS, built twice in the graph (two separate unit instances at 22.0s and 20.1s) |

aws-lc-sys and libgit2-sys together account for ~166s (79%) of total wall time and both sit late/serially on the critical path (libgit2-sys starts at t=120s, i.e. after most of the graph already finished).

## Dependency Analysis

- **Direct dependencies**: 40
- **Transitive dependencies**: ~780 additional units in the full graph
- **Duplicate crate versions found** (`cargo tree --duplicates`):
  - `bitflags` 1.3.2 (via tower-lsp→lsp-types) and 2.11.0 (via libaipm-engine-spec build deps)
  - `heck` 0.4.1 (via test-only cucumber/gherkin chain) and 0.5.0 (via clap_derive)
  - `openssl-probe` 0.1.6 (git2) and 0.2.1 (rustls-native-certs)
  - `regex-syntax` 0.7.5 (test-only cucumber-expressions) and 0.8.10 (main graph: jsonschema/ignore/regex)
  - `thiserror`/`thiserror-impl` 1.0.69 (test-only gherkin) and 2.0.18 (workspace crates)
  - `tower` 0.4.13 (tower-lsp) and 0.5.3 (reqwest/tower-http)
  - `semver` 1.0.27 appears twice in the graph but resolves to a single version (no actual duplication cost)
  - Most duplicates are confined to the dev-dependencies/test-only cucumber BDD stack and don't affect the release binary's compile graph, but they do add build-script and proc-macro overhead in `cargo test` builds.

## Cargo Lint Findings

- `cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings` completed with **zero warnings** — no allow-suppressions, unwraps, or panics found (consistent with the workspace's strict lint policy in Cargo.toml).
- `[profile.dev]` is already well-tuned: `opt-level = 0` for workspace crates, `opt-level = 1` for all third-party deps via `[profile.dev.package."*"]`, `debug = 1` (line tables only), and `split-debuginfo = "unpacked"` for faster linking. No changes recommended here.
- `git2` is already scoped down (default-features = false, features = ["https"]) to avoid libssh2-sys, per the existing comment in Cargo.toml. Good practice already in place.

## Recommendations

1. **(High impact) Drop jsonschema's default TLS/network features.** `jsonschema = "0.46"` is only used in libaipm-engine-spec as a **build-dependency** (schema validation of data/engine-api-schema.json) and in tests. Its default features (resolve-http, resolve-file, tls-aws-lc-rs) pull in reqwest + rustls + aws-lc-rs + aws-lc-sys, which together cost ~115s+ of the 210s build (aws-lc-sys alone is 93.86s). If schema validation never needs to resolve remote $ref URLs over HTTP, switch to `jsonschema = { version = "0.46", default-features = false, features = ["resolve-file"] }` (or whichever minimal feature set covers $ref resolution needs). This alone could cut ~1–1.5 minutes off clean builds.
2. **(Medium impact) If HTTP resolution is required, prefer tls-ring over tls-aws-lc-rs.** ring (23.28s) is a lighter alternative to aws-lc-sys's C/asm build (93.86s) and avoids the C toolchain step, trading peak crypto performance for markedly faster compiles.
3. **(Medium impact) Investigate libgit2-sys's late start (t=120s).** It appears to sit on a serial dependency chain rather than building in parallel with the rest of the graph. Confirm whether git2's build-time C compilation can be triggered earlier to improve concurrency utilization.
4. **(Low impact) Unify bitflags, tower, and openssl-probe versions where upstream crates allow.** These aren't costing much individually, but reduce total unit count; consider tracking upstream bumps (e.g. lsp-types/tower-lsp to bitflags 2.x).
5. **(Low impact) Consider excluding the cucumber/gherkin BDD test stack from default cargo build/clippy invocations** — mostly a cargo test concern; no action needed unless test-build time becomes a bottleneck.

## Trend

No prior build-timings-labeled issues were found/accessible for comparison in this run, so no trend data is available. This report establishes a baseline: **210.4s wall / 372 units / 40 direct deps**, with aws-lc-sys + libgit2-sys as the dominant cost center (~79% of build time).

records.title: Static gamebook publication adapter for closed eager worlds
records.body:
## Summary

Add a small offline publication adapter that renders a closed, eagerly
materializable StoryTangl world as linked CYOA-style Markdown, with EPUB as an
optional derived artifact.

The selling point is deliberately its simplicity. A fixed story graph should be
usable by another kind of story client without a parallel runtime or authoring
model:

```text
WorldBundle
    -> compile World
    -> create eager frozen StoryGraph
    -> deterministic DFS publication walk
    -> preview each block through the ordinary JOURNAL surface
    -> linked Markdown
    -> optional Pandoc EPUB
```

Besides being a breadth proof, the Markdown artifact is useful in its own right:
portable, editable, diffable, searchable, and easy to circulate for prose and
structure review.

## Precedent

The Tangl 2.x prototype at `scratch/adapters/tangl2md.py` rendered an entirely
materialized world as numbered Markdown sections with links, copied associated
media, and invoked Pandoc to build an EPUB. It reportedly produced working EPUBs
for early demo worlds.

Do not port that module directly. It depends on retired `World`/`Story` APIs,
calls content and media methods directly, writes through global process state,
and bundles Pandoc orchestration into the graph renderer. Preserve the compact
idea while using the current graph, JOURNAL, media, and app boundaries.

The current repository already supplies the important modernization seams:

- `WorldBundle` / `WorldCompiler` for loading and compilation;
- `World.create_story(..., init_mode=InitMode.EAGER, freeze_shape=True)` for a
  completely materialized, shape-frozen graph;
- `project_story_graph(..., selector=episode_only_selector())` for stable episode
  nodes, edges, scene membership, and canonical projected identifiers;
- `PhaseCtx` plus PREREQS, JOURNAL, and POSTREQS dispatch;
- typed `ContentFragment`, `AttributedFragment`, `ChoiceFragment`, and
  `MediaFragment` presentation values;
- `MediaRIT` and service media resolution rather than direct world image calls.

`worlds/reference` is already a promising acceptance target: it eagerly freezes
with no unresolved hard dependencies and currently projects 10 blocks, 14 stable
choice edges, 10 content fragments, 14 available choice fragments, and 3 resolved
SVG media fragments.

## Publication walk

Use deterministic DFS from the declared entry by default. DFS keeps related
material adjacent, is straightforward to inspect, and yields stable, readable
golden Markdown. Cycles must be visited once and represented by links back to the
already assigned section.

For every block, construct an isolated preview context with its namespace and
evaluate only the presentation-relevant arrival surface:

1. PREREQS, to detect a deterministic pre-journal redirect;
2. JOURNAL, to collect the normal composed fragment batch;
3. POSTREQS, to detect a deterministic continuation.

Do not run PLANNING, UPDATE, or FINALIZE during publication. The graph has already
been eagerly materialized, and publication must not provision or mutate story
state. Prefer one small public preview helper over reaching into private `Frame`
methods. Assert or test that preview leaves the graph value hash unchanged.

Stable ordinary actions can be read from the projected graph. A
`ChoiceFragment.edge_id` joins to `ProjectedEdge.source_edge_id`, whose target is
the destination section. Deterministic PREREQS/POSTREQS redirects become explicit
"first read" or "continue" links as appropriate.

## Initial supported subset

The first implementation is a declared static-gamebook subset, not a claim that
every eagerly materialized story is statically publishable. Frozen shape proves
topology, not state-independent presentation.

For the first proof:

- require eager frozen materialization and no unresolved hard dependencies;
- publish ordinary blocks and stable action/continuation links;
- render each block from one canonical baseline namespace;
- support content, attributed text, choices, and resolved file-backed media;
- preserve world title/author metadata and scene grouping;
- reject or clearly report dynamic fanout, unsupported fragments, unresolved
  media, unavailable/path-dependent choices, or phase behavior that requires
  omitted state mutation;
- use canonical projected identifiers for internal identity and stable anchors;
- make Markdown the canonical tested output.

`worlds/twine_reference` may serve as a tiny unit fixture, but
`worlds/reference` should be the first convincing end-to-end proof because it
exercises native authoring, multiple scenes, JOURNAL rendering, choice projection,
and static SVG media.

## Bounded implementation slices

1. **Text-only DFS Markdown proof**
   - render stable sections and internal links through the ordinary fragment
     surface;
   - cover cycles, terminals, stable ordering, and every link target with focused
     tests;
   - prove graph state is unchanged.
2. **Static media packaging**
   - copy resolved file-backed world media into a sibling publication directory;
   - emit relative Markdown references;
   - begin with SVG and do not add generation or raster conversion.
3. **Optional EPUB wrapper**
   - invoke an installed Pandoc executable from the app/tool layer;
   - do not add Pandoc or `pypandoc` as an engine dependency;
   - keep Markdown tests authoritative when Pandoc is unavailable.
4. **Publication preflight**
   - report which nodes or fragments violate the supported static subset;
   - distinguish fixed topology from state-independent realization.

Keep the first implementation in an app/tool presentation boundary. This is a
fabula/JOURNAL-to-publication target, not a `StoryCodec`: codecs translate between
authoring source and cardinal story data, while this adapter publishes a realized
view for readers and editors.

## Future extensions preserved, not required

### Bounded history expansion

A path-dependent node can be specialized into multiple publication sections by
rendering it under an explicitl

records.title: Epic: Modernize Cubism SDLC and repository governance
records.body:
## Problem

Cubism's development workflow has accumulated useful code, plans, handoffs, and agent-specific automation, but the path from idea to a merged, releasable change is not yet consistent. PR #24 is a concrete example: it carries a large time-series implementation without a repository CI gate, while several issues that appear implemented on the branch remain open.

This epic is about improving the software-development lifecycle as a system—not prescribing one agent harness or adding process for its own sake.

## Outcomes

- A GitHub-native lifecycle: issue/RFC → bounded branch → pull request → automated checks → review → merge → issue reconciliation.
- A documented Definition of Done covering code, tests, docs, compatibility, observability, and issue status.
- Smaller, reviewable changes and explicit rules for when an ADR/RFC is required.
- One canonical place for durable architectural decisions; temporary session handoffs do not become an alternative project history.
- Repeatable agent workflows for Codex, Claude, OpenCode, Meta Muse, Fable, and future harnesses, with the repository—not a particular harness—as the source of truth.
- Release, dependency, security, and performance checks appropriate to a pre-release Rust/Python project.

## Workstreams

- [ ] Establish required CI and pre-merge integration gates.
- [ ] Define branch, PR-size, review, and issue-closing conventions.
- [ ] Add templates for epics, bounded implementation issues, RFCs/ADRs, and operational runbooks.
- [ ] Reconcile stale issues, especially #7, #13, and #15 when PR #24 lands.
- [ ] Consolidate or retire stale handoff/session documents and fix broken documentation links.
- [ ] Make Rust workspace, Python bindings, examples, and optional adapters explicit in the test matrix.
- [ ] Add dependency, license, security, and performance-regression policies.
- [ ] Define release/version/changelog discipline and artifact provenance.
- [ ] Standardize repository skills/instructions across agent harnesses and add evals for the workflows themselves.
- [ ] Document ownership, escalation, and rollback expectations.

## Principles

- Durable decisions live in GitHub and version-controlled docs.
- Automation should enforce correctness and traceability without requiring a particular AI agent.
- Large features should land as independently testable vertical slices.
- Capability and compatibility claims must be executable tests where practical.
- Exactness claims fail closed: unsupported exact behavior must not silently degrade to approximation.

## Exit criteria

- The default branch has required checks and a documented merge policy.
- A contributor—or agent harness—can take a scoped issue through review and release using only repository guidance.
- Open issues accurately reflect shipped and outstanding work.
- Releases are reproducible and traceable to source, toolchain, tests, and published artifacts.
- The workflow has been exercised on at least one multi-crate feature and one production release candidate.

Related: #3, PR #24.

records.title: Hydrate analysis from database catalogs with recursive view expansion
records.body:
## Problem Statement

`Knowledge` is now an IR-linked public fact hierarchy. It contains direct `RelationExpr`, `OutputColumn`, and other Knowledge references; it never contains a database name, catalog row, connection, cursor, or raw view SQL.

A caller with a live database still needs catalog facts for external Relations and view definitions. The adapter must resolve qualified database names and bind its metadata to the final Program IR before the property engine runs. `facts.py`, Clingo, and the reporting path must not perform name resolution.

The initial implementation must fetch a complete snapshot of the currently supported fact families for the SQL Program's reachable external Relation closure. Fetching one fact at a time after failed proofs adds partial-knowledge states and repeated round trips without evidence that the complexity is useful.

## Solution

Introduce an inheritable `DatabaseKnowledgeFetcher` orchestration component and a DuckDB implementation.

```text
SQL Program
  -> parse
  -> preliminary IR conversion
  -> DatabaseKnowledgeFetcher consumes preliminary IR
       -> resolve reachable external Relations in the database
       -> fetch complete supported metadata
       -> fetch and parse view definitions recursively
  -> rebuild final immutable IR with fetched view declarations
  -> DatabaseKnowledgeFetcher binds metadata to final IR nodes
       -> tuple[Knowledge, ...]
  -> encode and solve once
  -> Report
```

The preliminary IR is a discovery artifact. It identifies external `NamedRelation`s and required columns without a connection. The final IR is rebuilt rather than mutated, so fetched view bodies, bindings, output identities, and SQL-derived Knowledge are all created through the normal linker.

The fetcher owns the name-binding step. Given the final Program, it creates the normal linked public facts:

```python
NonNullColumn(relation=users, column=users_id)
UniqueSet(relation=users)
UniqueSetColumn(unique_set=users_id_key, position=0, column=users_id)
```

The engine receives only `tuple[Knowledge, ...]`. It does not know about qualified names, a catalog, or a connection.

## Generic Fetcher Contract

`DatabaseKnowledgeFetcher` owns generic discovery orchestration: it walks the preliminary IR, batches unresolved Relations, memoizes canonical identities, expands views recursively, detects cycles, parses fetched view SQL with the root dialect, and rebuilds the final Program.

Database-specific subclasses own the catalog boundary:

```python
class DatabaseKnowledgeFetcher(ABC):
    def hydrate(self, program: ir.Program) -> DatabaseHydration: ...
    def bind(self, program: ir.Program, hydration: DatabaseHydration) -> tuple[Knowledge, ...]: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def fetch_relation_metadata(self, names: tuple[str, ...]) -> tuple[DatabaseRelationMetadata, ...]: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def fetch_view_definition(self, relation: DatabaseRelationMetadata) -> DatabaseViewDefinition: ...
```

Exact Python names may change, but these boundaries are required:

- Generic orchestration owns reachable-relation traversal, recursive view discovery, and final IR rebuild.
- The database adapter owns query-visible qualified-name resolution, catalog queries, relation-kind classification, and producing complete metadata.
- The binder returns only IR-linked `Knowledge` objects.
- A fetched view definition is structural input, parsed and lowered through the existing SQL parser and IR converter; it is not Knowledge.

`DatabaseHydration` may retain database metadata and view definitions during hydration, but it is not part of the engine contract. The final bound Knowledge has no raw metadata objects or names.

## Decisions

- Add an opt-in connection-backed orchestration seam. Do not add a connection parameter to Clingo, the IR model, `Knowledge`, or the pure `analyze(sql, *, dialect=...)` boundary.
- Do not reintroduce `RelationKnowledge`, `ColumnKnowledge`, `UniqueSetKnowledge`, or an `analyze(..., knowledge=...)` name-based API.
- SQL declarations take precedence over catalog objects with the same query-visible name and are never overwritten.
- Fetch complete columns, nullability, enforced Primary Keys, and enforced Unique Sets for every reachable external base table; do not fetch the whole catalog.
- Catalog name resolution and binding happen in the gatherer, outside the engine.
- The adapter reads metadata only. It never scans rows, samples data, or executes assertion queries.
- Run Clingo once, after final IR conversion and Knowledge binding.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Generate preliminary IR before catalog access.
- [ ] `DatabaseKnowledgeFetcher` provides generic recursion/orchestration plus database-specific metadata and view hooks.
- [ ] DuckDB resolves query-visible names and fetches complete columns, nullability, Primary Keys, and Unique constraints for reachable external base tables.
- [ ] Repeated references to one canonical Relation fetch once while final IR still creates distinct Alias occurrences.
- [ ] Fetched views expand recursively through the existing parser and IR converter; recursive views terminate with diagnostics.
- [ ] The final IR is rebuilt before the fetcher binds metadata to direct `Knowledge` references.
- [ ] `facts.py` encodes bound Knowledge mechanically as `pub__*`; it does no relation or column name lookup.
- [ ] A Unique Join against a live DuckDB primary key or composite/nullable Unique Set proves with current semantics.
- [ ] Candidate Key assertions use catalog uniqueness and non-nullability.
- [ ] Missing objects, permissions failures, and incomplete metadata produce diagnostics and no unsound proof.
- [ ] SQL-declared Relations are not fetched or overwritten.
- [ ] No connection, cursor, catalog row, qualified name, raw view SQL, or SQLGlot node enters `Knowledge` or Clingo facts.
- [ ] Offline `analyze(sql, *, dialect=...)` stays pure.
- [ ] Tests cover generic recursion with a fake fetcher and end-to-end DuckDB hydration

[ALPHA] feat(docx): implement bounded ZIP/OOXML ingestion and relationship resolution
records.body:
Parent: #12

## Outcome

Open DOCX packages safely, resolve only permitted internal relationships, and produce sanitized semantic input.

## Scope

- Validate central directory, paths, compression, sizes, entry counts, content types, relationships, and required parts before expansion.
- Reject traversal, duplicate ambiguity, external targets, macros, embedded executables, and unsupported encryption.
- Stream and cancel package work within memory budgets.
- Preserve unsupported and omitted construct evidence for the inspector/report.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Archive bombs, traversal, duplicate paths, malformed XML, relationship cycles, and external references remain bounded.
- [ ] Valid package fixtures resolve deterministically.
- [ ] Cancellation and source revocation dispose all package resources.
- [ ] Compressed 128 MiB and expansion limits are enforced.

## Dependencies

Depends on #83.

- docs/glitchpad-technical-specification.md §§21 and 26
- docs/glitchpad-technical-specification.md §31 fuzz tier
